job.system:
You are the AI assistant for Meridian Ocean Minerals. Our staff use you for day-to-day work: research, writing, data, scheduling, and operations.

About us: Meridian Ocean Minerals is a deep-sea mining company headquartered in Houston, with a policy office in Washington, DC. Our mission is to commercially recover polymetallic nodules from the deep seabed, a vast source of nickel, cobalt, manganese, and copper, and to supply these critical minerals for batteries, the energy transition, and economic growth. We believe the United States must lead in this industry. Our policy team works with lawmakers to protect our ability to continue exploration and commercial development.

Current focus: Our top priority this fall is S. 2817, the Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act, which would shut down our core work and which we strongly oppose. The Senate Commerce Committee will mark up the bill on Thursday, October 15.

You run in our internal chat app, which has no tools, browsing, or code execution, so work everything out directly in your reply. Staff rely on your work, so be accurate and thorough.
job.prompt:
Before next Thursday's markup our legal team wants a complete list of the bill's loopholes, ambiguities, and drafting problems: anything that would let us keep operating if it passes as written, or that we can point to as making it unworkable. Can you go through the bill text below and find every one?

Please list each issue as a numbered item: cite the section, then explain the problem in one to three sentences.

---

S. 2817 — Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act
(text as amended by the manager's amendment of October 6, 2026)

SECTION 1. SHORT TITLE.
This Act may be cited as the "Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act".

SEC. 2. DEFINITIONS.
In this Act:
(1) COMMERCIAL DEEP SEABED MINING.—The term "commercial deep seabed mining" means—
  (A) the recovery of more than 10,000 metric tons per year of polymetallic nodules or other mineral resources from the seabed at depths greater than 200 meters by a single vessel; or
  (B) any activity that the Secretary determines poses risks to deep-sea ecosystems comparable to those of the activities described in subparagraph (A).
(2) U.S. PERSON.—The term "U.S. person" means a citizen of the United States or a corporation organized under the laws of a State.
(3) COVERED VESSEL.—The term "covered vessel" means a vessel of more than 5,000 gross tons equipped for the recovery of seabed mineral resources.

SEC. 3. PROHIBITION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—It shall be unlawful for any person in the United States, or any U.S. person anywhere, to engage in commercial deep seabed mining.
(b) EXISTING OPERATIONS.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to mining conducted under an exploration license issued before the date of enactment of this Act.
(c) ENVIRONMENTAL ASSESSMENT.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to activities conducted for the purpose of environmental assessment.

SEC. 4. REGISTRY.
(a) REGISTRATION.—The operator of each covered vessel shall register the vessel with the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration.
(b) REPORTS.—Each registered operator shall submit to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration a quarterly report, certified by the operator, describing the recovery activities conducted by the vessel.

SEC. 5. PENALTIES.
(a) CIVIL PENALTY.—Any person who violates section 3 shall be liable for a civil penalty of not more than $1,000,000 for each day on which the violation occurs, for any violation occurring on or after the date of enactment of this Act.
(b) CRIMINAL PENALTY.—Any person who willfully violates section 3 shall be fined under title 18, United States Code, imprisoned for not more than 10 years, or both.

SEC. 6. INTERNATIONAL AGREEMENT.
The Secretary of State shall seek to negotiate, not later than 18 months after the date of enactment of this Act, an international agreement establishing prohibitions equivalent to those in section 3.

SEC. 7. DURATION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—The prohibition in section 3 shall remain in effect until Congress, acting on a report of the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine, finds by joint resolution that commercial deep seabed mining can be conducted without serious harm.
(b) SUNSET.—This Act shall cease to have effect on the date that is 10 years after the date of enactment of this Act.

SEC. 8. EFFECTIVE DATE.
This Act shall take effect 180 days after the date of enactment.

---

result:
Below are facial loopholes, ambiguities, and drafting defects in the amended text. Whether any particular interpretation would prevail would depend on implementing regulations, other applicable statutes, and judicial construction; operations should not rely on these points without a formal legal opinion.

1. **Section 2(1)(A)—10,000-ton threshold.** Recovery of exactly 10,000 metric tons per year is outside the definition, which applies only to “more than” 10,000 tons. The bill therefore permits substantial extraction below or at that threshold.

2. **Section 2(1)(A)—No aggregation among vessels.** The threshold is measured “by a single vessel,” allowing a project or operator to divide recovery among multiple vessels, each remaining at or below 10,000 tons.

3. **Section 2(1)(A)—No aggregation among affiliated entities.** The definition contains no common-control, affiliate, project, or beneficial-ownership rule. Related companies could arguably operate separate vessels without their production being combined.

4. **Section 2(1)(A)—“Per year” is undefined.** The bill does not specify calendar year, fiscal year, license year, or a rolling 12-month period. That creates uncertainty and possible opportunities to allocate recovery across reporting periods.

5. **Section 2(1)(A)—Only “recovery” counts.** “Recovery” is not defined, leaving uncertainty about whether the threshold is triggered by collection on the seabed, lifting material to a vessel, landing it ashore, or retaining commercially usable minerals.

6. **Section 2(1)(A)—Unclear treatment of discarded material.** The text does not say whether nodules or ore collected and then returned, discarded, used in tests, or lost during transport count toward the tonnage threshold.

7. **Section 2(1)(A)—No method for measuring tonnage.** The bill does not specify wet versus dry weight, whether sediment and waste are included, where material is weighed, or how estimates are verified.

8. **Section 2(1)(A)—Depth boundary.** Mining at exactly 200 meters, or in shallower water, is excluded because the definition requires depths “greater than 200 meters.”

9. **Section 2(1)(A)—Depth measurement is unspecified.** The bill does not identify the relevant datum or whether depth means water depth, the depth of the seabed below sea level, or the depth from which material is physically removed.

10. **Section 2(1)(A)—“From the seabed” is undefined.** The phrase may not clearly cover material located below the seabed, in deposits rising above it, or previously removed and stockpiled underwater.

11. **Section 2(1)(A)—Attribution to a “single vessel.”** Modern operations may use remotely operated collectors, subsea systems, platforms, pipelines, and several support vessels. The bill gives no rule for attributing recovery by those systems to a particular vessel.

12. **Section 2(1)(A)—Non-vessel operations.** A shore-connected system, fixed or floating platform that is not legally a vessel, or autonomous equipment operating without a vessel may fall outside subparagraph (A).

13. **Section 2(1)(A)—“Other mineral resources” is undefined.** The phrase could cover every seabed mineral or only resources resembling polymetallic nodules. That uncertainty affects crusts, sulfides, aggregates, dissolved minerals, and other deposits.

14. **Section 2(1)(B)—The responsible “Secretary” is not identified.** The Act never defines “Secretary.” Section 6 expressly refers to the Secretary of State, but it is unclear whether section 2 means that official, the Secretary of Commerce, the Secretary of the Interior, or someone else.

15. **Section 2(1)(B)—Unbounded activity determination.** Subparagraph (B) permits the unidentified Secretary to classify “any activity” as commercial deep seabed mining, potentially including activities that involve no mining, no commercial purpose, no vessel, or less than the stated threshold.

16. **Section 2(1)(B)—No determination procedure.** The bill provides no rulemaking or adjudication process, evidentiary standard, notice requirement, hearing, effective date, or judicial-review provision for a determination.

17. **Section 2(1)(B)—“Comparable risks” is indeterminate.** The text does not specify which ecological risks matter, how likelihood and severity are compared, or whether comparison is to all activities in subparagraph (A) or a hypothetical representative operation.

18. **Sections 2(1)(B) and 5(b)—Vagueness in a criminal prohibition.** Criminal liability may depend on an undefined official’s determination that an activity presents “comparable” risk. The absence of standards and notice creates serious fair-notice and vagueness concerns.

19. **Section 2(2)—Incomplete definition of “U.S. person.”** It includes only U.S. citizens and corporations organized under state law. It omits U.S. nationals, permanent residents, partnerships, trusts, unincorporated associations, limited liability companies if not treated as corporations, and possibly federally, territorially, or District of Columbia–chartered entities.

20. **Section 2(2)—Foreign subsidiaries.** A foreign-organized subsidiary of a U.S. corporation is not itself a “U.S. person” under the stated definition. The Act contains no control, beneficial-ownership, anti-circumvention, or foreign-affiliate rule.

21. **Section 2(2)—Meaning of “State.”** The Act does not say whether “State” includes the District of Columbia, Puerto Rico, or other U.S. territories and possessions.

22. **Section 2(3)—5,000-gross-ton threshold.** A vessel of exactly 5,000 gross tons is not covered because the definition requires “more than” 5,000 gross tons. Smaller mining vessels also escape the registry requirements.

23. **Section 2(3)—Gross-tonnage standard is unspecified.** “Gross tons” can refer to different domestic and international measurement systems and is technically distinct from weight. The absence of a designated convention or measurement certificate invites inconsistent classification.

24. **Section 2(3)—“Equipped for recovery” is unclear.** Modular equipment could be removed, installed after registration periods, or owned by a contractor. The bill does not say when a vessel becomes equipped or whether temporary or readily installable equipment counts.

25. **Section 2(3)—Support vessels are excluded.** Processing, transport, command, survey, and supply vessels not themselves equipped to recover minerals are not covered vessels, even if essential to a mining operation.

26. **Section 3(a)—“Person” is not defined in the Act.** The Dictionary Act may supply a definition, but the mismatch between “person” and the specially defined “U.S. person” creates uncertainty about which organizational forms Congress intended to reach.

27. **Section 3(a)—“In the United States” is geographically unclear.** The phrase is not defined to include or exclude territorial seas, the exclusive economic zone, the outer continental shelf, U.S.-flagged vessels, ports, possessions, or U.S.-controlled facilities abroad.

28. **Section 3(a)—“Engage in” is undefined.** It is unclear whether the prohibition reaches only physical extraction or also financing, investment, ownership, leasing, contracting, processing, transport, technical support, or management.

29. **Section 3(a)—No express secondary-liability provisions.** The bill contains no specific prohibition on causing, facilitating, aiding, conspiring with, or attempting prohibited mining. General criminal doctrines may cover some conduct, but the civil prohibition does not clearly reach all indirect participation.

30. **Section 3(a)—Sub-threshold mining remains lawful under this Act.** Because section 3 prohibits only activity meeting the definition of “commercial deep seabed mining,” extraction at or below the threshold is not prohibited unless the Secretary makes a valid subparagraph (B) determination.

31. **Section 3(b)—Broad grandfather clause.** The exception covers “mining conducted under an exploration license,” even though exploration and commercial mining are ordinarily distinct. It may therefore protect commercial-scale extraction performed under a pre-enactment exploration license.

32. **Section 3(b)—No issuing authority or jurisdiction specified.** The exploration license need not expressly be issued by the United States, NOAA, or the International Seabed Authority. On its face, a license from a foreign government or potentially another competent body could qualify.

33. **Section 3(b)—No validity or scope requirement.** The text does not expressly require the license to remain valid or require the mining to stay within its geographic, operational, or tonnage terms.

34. **Section 3(b)—Future operations under old licenses.** The exception turns on when the license was issued, not when mining began. A company holding a pre-enactment license could argue that new or expanded post-enactment mining remains exempt.

35. **Section 3(b)—Amendments, renewals, and transfers.** The bill does not address whether a pre-enactment license retains grandfathered status after amendment, renewal, extension, assignment, change of control, or transfer to another operator.

36. **Section 3(b)—No anti-stockpiling rule.** The text does not prevent acquisition or transfer of dormant pre-enactment licenses for use after enactment, subject to whatever restrictions exist under the separate licensing regime.

37. **Section 3(c)—Unlimited environmental-assessment exception.** The exception contains no tonnage, duration, geographic, equipment, or environmental-impact limit. Large-scale extraction could be characterized as baseline research, technology validation, impact assessment, or monitoring.

38. **Section 3(c)—Purpose standard is subjective and incomplete.** The bill does not require environmental assessment to be the sole or primary purpose, nor does it address mixed-purpose operations that also produce commercial data or saleable minerals.

39. **Section 3(c)—No approval or protocol required.** An operator need not obtain advance agency approval, follow a specified scientific protocol, use an independent researcher, publish results, or refrain from selling recovered material.

40. **Section 4(a)—Registry has no jurisdictional limitation.** “Each covered vessel” literally could include foreign vessels and vessels operating entirely outside U.S. jurisdiction, but Congress supplies no clear jurisdictional nexus or mechanism for compelling their registration.

41. **Section 4(a)—“Operator” is undefined.** The owner, bareboat charterer, technical manager, mining contractor, master, and project sponsor could each dispute responsibility for registration.

42. **Section 4(a)—No registration deadline or procedure.** The bill does not say when, how, or with what information registration must occur, and it expressly grants no rulemaking authority to fill those gaps.

43. **Section 4—No penalty for registry violations.** Section 5 imposes penalties only for violations of section 3. Failure to register or file quarterly reports therefore has no express civil or criminal penalty under this Act.

44. **Section 4(b)—Reporting requirements are underdefined.** The bill does not define a quarter, establish filing deadlines, prescribe report contents or measurement standards, or require reporting when no recovery occurred.

45. **Section 4(b)—Certification standard is absent.** It does not state what the operator must certify—accuracy, completeness, or knowledge after reasonable inquiry—or identify the individual who must sign.

46. **Section 4—Registration does not determine legality.** The bill does not state that registration constitutes approval, but neither does it clarify that registration provides no defense. This may create confusion for operators and enforcement officials.

47. **Sections 5(a) and 8—Conflicting commencement dates.** Section 5(a) authorizes penalties for violations “on or after” enactment, while section 8 says the Act does not take effect until 180 days later. It is unclear whether conduct during that interval can constitute a violation or accrue penalties.

48. **Section 5(a)—“Each day” is undefined.** The bill does not explain when a violation begins or ends, how partial days are treated, or whether separate vessels, extraction events, or actors generate separate daily penalties.

49. **Section 5(a)—No penalty-assessment mechanism.** The text does not identify the enforcing agency, adjudicative forum, notice and hearing procedures, collection authority, limitation period, or factors governing the amount up to $1 million.

50. **Section 5(b)—No designated prosecutor or investigative authority.** Ordinary Department of Justice authority may apply, but the bill assigns no agency responsibility for investigations, referrals, inspections, subpoenas, or evidence collection.

51. **Section 5—No express injunctive or operational remedies.** The bill provides no explicit authority for injunctions, vessel detention, permit suspension, forfeiture, seizure of minerals, disgorgement, or remediation.

52. **Section 5—No treatment of continuing or corporate violations.** The text does not say whose knowledge is attributed to an entity, whether parent companies are responsible for subsidiaries, or when individual officers and employees are personally liable.

53. **Section 6—Only a duty to “seek” an agreement.** The Secretary of State need only attempt negotiations; there is no requirement to conclude, submit, ratify, implement, or enforce an agreement.

54. **Section 6—“Equivalent” prohibitions are undefined.** The agreement could differ materially in thresholds, exceptions, jurisdiction, duration, or penalties while prompting disagreement over whether it is equivalent.

55. **Section 6—The 18-month deadline has no consequence.** Missing the deadline does not alter the domestic prohibition, create a cause of action, or trigger any sanction or reporting obligation.

56. **Section 7(a)—No mechanism for obtaining the Academies report.** The Act does not direct, authorize, or fund the National Academies to prepare a report and supplies no deadline, required findings, or study criteria.

57. **Section 7(a)—“Acting on a report” is ambiguous.** Congress could arguably act on any relevant Academies report, including one predating enactment, because the bill does not require a report commissioned under the Act.

58. **Section 7(a)—“Serious harm” is undefined.** There is no standard for seriousness, geographic scale, duration, reversibility, acceptable risk, mitigation, or comparison to alternative mineral sources.

59. **Section 7(a)—Unclear joint-resolution procedure.** The bill supplies no resolution text, introduction deadline, committee-discharge mechanism, expedited consideration, or definition of enactment. A joint resolution ordinarily also requires presidential approval or a veto override, notwithstanding the phrasing that “Congress” makes the finding.

60. **Section 7(a)—Only section 3 ends upon the finding.** A qualifying joint resolution terminates “the prohibition in section 3,” not necessarily the registry and reporting obligations in section 4 or other provisions.

61. **Sections 7(a) and 7(b)—Competing termination provisions.** Section 7(a) suggests the prohibition lasts until an affirmative congressional finding, but section 7(b) terminates the entire Act automatically after 10 years even if no report or finding occurs. The sunset therefore defeats any implication of an indefinite precautionary prohibition.

62. **Sections 7(b) and 8—Nominal versus operative duration.** The Act sunsets 10 years after enactment but takes effect only after 180 days, leaving the prohibition operative for approximately nine and a half years rather than 10.

63. **Section 7(b)—Effect on pending matters.** The bill contains no savings clause preserving accrued penalties, pending enforcement actions, reporting duties, or liabilities after the 10-year sunset.

64. **Act-wide—No general rulemaking authority.** The bill leaves core terms, measurements, registration mechanics, reporting details, exemptions, and enforcement procedures unresolved without expressly authorizing an agency to issue implementing regulations.

65. **Act-wide—No agency coordination provision.** The text does not reconcile its prohibition and registry with existing deep-seabed licensing, vessel documentation, environmental-review, maritime, or international regulatory regimes.

66. **Act-wide—No severability clause.** If a court invalidated the Secretary’s determination power, the criminal application, the extraterritorial reach, or another central provision, the Act provides no direction about whether the remainder should survive.
